How to decode a JWT without a tool

A JWT's header and payload are just base64url-encoded JSON — no library, no website, and no secret key required to read them. Here is exactly how, and where the technique stops working.

Step 1: split on the dots

A JWT (technically a JWS in compact serialization) is three base64url segments joined by periods: header.payload.signature. Splitting on . gives you the three pieces to work with. If you don't get exactly three, what you're looking at either isn't a JWT or has been truncated somewhere — a real token always has exactly two dots.

Step 2: undo the URL-safe substitution and re-add padding

Standard base64 uses + and /, both of which are meaningful inside a URL. Since JWTs routinely travel in URLs and headers, they use the base64url variant instead: swap every - back to + and every _ back to /. Base64url also drops the trailing = padding that standard base64 requires, so add it back: pad the segment with = characters until its length is a multiple of 4. 

segment.length % 4 === 2  -> add "=="
segment.length % 4 === 3  -> add "="
segment.length % 4 === 0  -> no padding needed

Step 3: base64-decode and read the JSON

Once you have standard, padded base64, any base64 decoder recovers the original bytes, which are UTF-8 text encoding a JSON object. In a shell: 

echo '<padded, +/-substituted header segment>' | base64 -d

In a browser console, the built-in atob() does the same thing for a payload without any embedded Unicode outside the ASCII range: JSON.parse(atob(paddedSegment)). Do this for both the header and the payload segments; you now have two readable JSON objects with no library, no website, and no key of any kind.

Why the signature segment is different

The third segment is not encoded JSON — it's the raw output bytes of a cryptographic signature (an HMAC digest, or an RSA/ECDSA signature) computed over the first two segments. Running it through the same decode steps above gives you back binary data with no JSON structure to recover, because there was never a JSON object encoded into it in the first place. Reading the header and payload tells you what the token claims; only verifying the signature against the correct key tells you whether those claims can be trusted, and that step needs a real JWT library and the key — there is no by-hand shortcut for it, and there shouldn't be one.

What a clean decode does and doesn't tell you

Decoding recovers exactly what was written into the token, nothing more. Anyone can hand-craft a header and payload that decode perfectly cleanly — a well-formed, readable JSON payload is not evidence the token is genuine, current, or intended for the service reading it. That's the gap this checker is built for: once you can read a token's claims, it also flags the specific structural patterns worth a second look — alg: none, an embedded key header, a suspiciously long lifetime, a sensitive-looking field name — the same read-through either way, just with the known failure shapes already checked for you.

Common questions

Do I need the secret key to decode a JWT?

No. The header and payload are base64url-encoded, not encrypted -- decoding them back to readable JSON needs no key at all. The secret or private key is only involved in verifying the signature segment (proving the token was not tampered with), which is a completely separate step from reading the claims.

Why can't I decode the third segment the same way?

The third segment is the raw signature bytes -- a cryptographic output, not encoded JSON. Running it through a base64url decoder gives you back binary data with no readable structure, because there was never a JSON object encoded into it to recover. It exists to be verified against the header and payload using a key, not to be read.

Why does base64url use - and _ instead of + and /?

Standard base64 uses + and /, both of which have special meaning in a URL (query separators and path segments). JWTs are routinely passed in URLs and HTTP headers, so RFC 7519 specifies the URL-safe base64url variant, which substitutes - for + and _ for /, and drops the trailing = padding characters entirely. A generic base64 decoder that doesn't know this will fail or produce garbage on a real JWT segment until you swap those characters back and re-add padding.

Does a clean decode mean the token is valid?

No. Decoding only recovers the claims that were written into the token -- it proves nothing about whether those claims are genuine. A token with a completely invalid or missing signature decodes exactly as cleanly as a correctly signed one; anyone can hand-craft a header and payload that decode perfectly. Only verifying the signature against the correct key, using a real JWT library, proves the token wasn't tampered with.

JWT Security Check

Paste a JSON Web Token and get its header and payload decoded instantly, plus every common security misconfiguration flagged: alg: none, embedded key headers, algorithm-confusion risk, a suspicious kid, timing-claim problems, and sensitive-looking payload fields.

No signature verification, no upload. This tool never asks for a key and never verifies a signature -- it only decodes the header/payload (no key needed for that) and checks them against a documented list of misconfiguration patterns. A finding is something worth a look, not a verdict, and a clean result is not a guarantee your token or server is secure.

    Usage is optional, stays in this browser, and counts only that a check ran or a summary was copied. The token you paste, its decoded contents, and every finding are never recorded, uploaded, or sent to an analytics service. Uncheck to turn it off. Do Not Track and Global Privacy Control disable counting automatically.

    Common questions

    Does this tool verify the JWT's signature?

    No, and it never asks for a key to do so. It only decodes the header and payload (which need no key -- they are base64url-encoded, not encrypted) and checks them for documented misconfiguration patterns. Verifying a signature requires the actual signing key or public key, which this tool never requests, stores, or needs.

    Is my token uploaded anywhere?

    No. Every check runs entirely in your browser, in JavaScript. The token you paste, its decoded contents, and every finding never leave your device -- there is no server-side processing and no third-party analytics vendor.

    What does alg: none mean and why is it flagged?

    "none" is a real, spec-defined algorithm value (RFC 7518) for an explicitly unsigned token. A verifier that accepts it treats the token as valid with no signature check at all -- a well-documented forgery technique, since anyone can hand-craft a header and payload and set alg to none. This tool flags it as high severity whenever it appears.

    Is a clean result a guarantee the token or my server is secure?

    No. Every check here is a structural, pattern-matching signal against a documented list of known failure shapes -- not a full security audit, and not a claim about your verifying code, which this tool never sees. A token with zero findings can still be misused by an insecure verifier, and a token that trips a finding can still be handled safely by correct verification code. Read every finding as worth a look, not a verdict.

vs-eyeballing-the-payload.html.text:
JWT Security Check · comparison

JWT Security Check vs. eyeballing the payload

Pasting the two segments into a base64 decoder and reading the resulting JSON genuinely catches an obviously wrong claim value. This page names no specific decoder site or library — decoding a token and reading it by eye is a habit most developers already have, not a competing tool.

What eyeballing the decoded claims catches reliably

A claim that is obviously the wrong value, a typo'd field name, a role or permission that plainly should not be there — anything that looks wrong once you can read the JSON is exactly what a careful reviewer is good at noticing. This tool does not replace that kind of reading.

What eyeballing the decoded claims cannot catch, by construction

CaseReading it decoded, by eyeThis tool
"alg": "none"A real, spec-defined field value — reads as an ordinary field, not an error, unless you already know to distrust it on sightFlags it as high severity every time, with the specific consequence named: a verifier accepting it skips signature verification entirely
An embedded jwk, or a jku/x5u key URL, in the headerDecodes to well-formed JSON — a key object or a URL string, exactly as the spec describes; nothing about the decoded value itself signals riskNames the specific header-injection attack surface each field creates if the verifier trusts it uncritically
A symmetric algorithm alongside an embedded asymmetric key hintTwo separate, individually ordinary-looking fields; recognizing the combination as the documented "algorithm confusion" shape takes knowing to look for itFlags the combination specifically, by name, with the mechanism explained
A kid value shaped like ../../etc/passwd or 1' OR '1'='1Decodes to an ordinary-looking string; nothing marks it as a path-traversal or SQL-injection shape rather than a normal opaque identifierPattern-matches the value against both shapes and names which one it resembles
An excessively long lifetime (exp minus iat)Both are just numbers — recognizing "40 days" as unusually long for an access token requires doing the subtraction and knowing a reference point to compare it againstComputes the lifetime and flags it against a stated, documented reference point

The gap that matters most: the risk lives in the verifying code, not in the decoded text

This isn't a case of a reviewer missing something a more careful read could have caught. Every field above decodes to perfectly well-formed, ordinary-looking JSON — that is exactly what makes each one easy to miss. Whether alg: none is actually dangerous, whether an embedded jwk is actually trusted, whether a long lifetime is actually a problem: all of that depends on code you cannot see by decoding the token, which is the verifying service's own logic. A mechanical check against the exact list of documented patterns, rather than a read of whether the values look plausible, is not a more careful version of reading the payload; it is a different question asked of the same text.

When to still read the decoded claims yourself

This tool only reports the specific patterns on its list, in the header and payload you paste. It is not a security audit, it never verifies a signature, and it never sees your server's verification code — so it cannot tell you whether a jwk header is actually trusted, or whether a role claim is the right one for this user. Judging whether the token's actual business content is correct is still a job for reading the decoded claims yourself.

Common questions

What does eyeballing a decoded JWT actually catch?

A reviewer catches what looks obviously wrong once decoded: a claim value that is clearly the wrong user, a typo'd field name, a role that should not be there. Those are real problems and a careful read finds them the same way it always has. This tool does not replace that kind of reading -- it looks for a narrower, more specific class of problem that decoding alone does not surface.

Why doesn't alg: none look wrong when you read it?

Because "none" is a real, spec-defined value (RFC 7518) for an explicitly unsigned token -- it reads as a normal field with a normal-looking value, not as an error. The problem is not that the field looks malformed; it is that a verifier accepting this value skips signature verification entirely, and that consequence lives in the verifying code, not in anything visible in the decoded header.

Why doesn't an embedded jwk or jku header look wrong?

A jwk (embedded key) or jku (key URL) field decodes to perfectly well-formed JSON -- a key object or a URL string, exactly as the spec describes. Nothing about the decoded value itself signals danger. The risk is entirely about what the verifying code does with it: whether it trusts a key the token itself supplied instead of only its own configured key store, which a read of the decoded JSON cannot tell you either way.

Why is a kid header injection shape easy to miss by eye?

A kid value like "../../etc/passwd" or "1' OR '1'='1" decodes to a completely ordinary-looking JSON string. Recognizing it as a path-traversal or SQL-injection shape requires knowing those specific patterns and actively checking for them -- a plain read-through of the claims, focused on whether the data looks right, has no reason to flag a string field for its shape rather than its content.

Does a clean check mean the token and its verifier are secure?

No. This tool only reports the specific, named patterns it checks for in the header and payload you paste. It never verifies a signature and never sees your server's verification code, so a clean result means none of its checks fired -- not that the token or the service issuing or verifying it is secure.
